It’s four answers to four questions. Here we go…
h
1. How do we fire someone in an office with no privacy?
q

I’m curious for your opinion on the kindest way to deliver the news that someone is losing their job. My direct report is being let go because of performance concerns, being a poor fit for the role, and making errors. She’s been told about these concerns directly and hasn’t shown improvement. We’ve decided it’s time to terminate her.
q

We work a hybrid schedule (two days in office), and our office is a big open space with only glass conference rooms. Doing this over Zoom and coordinating supply returns feels cowardly and cold. Doing it in the office with the rest of the staff there feels cruel. We’re thinking about asking her to come in early to have this conversation, allow her to collect her belongings/ return company items and leave before everyone else arrives. I’m assuming the meeting request will tip her off, but it seems like the kindest way to handle this. Are we overthinking it?
p
Ugh, I think asking someone to get up early just to be fired is kind of crappy too.
p

None of the options are good! I’d either do it first thing in the morning at her normal time of arrival, or have the conversation via Zoom (which is how it has to be done when people work from other states anyway). I know you’re worried that doing it by Zoom feels cold, but it might be more humane than bringing her in specifically to fire her with a bunch of people around.
p

And this is one of many reasons why even open-plan offices need to have some private meeting spaces. There are lots of types of bad news that need to be delivered at work sometimes, or other conversations that require privacy. Even just putting some blinds on some of the conference room windows would help.
p

Related:
how do we handle firing an employee in an open plan office?

2. Copilot cited my meeting remarks as a source of information to another team
q

We have an enterprise license for Copilot, albeit with guardrails that (supposedly) keep all of our information internal to our network. I’ve never found it helpful or accurate despite several good-faith attempts at using it, so I mostly leave it alone. Our organization employs over 40,000 people in various roles.
q

Earlier today, my boss called me to ask about something I supported in a previous role. He said he first tried to ask Copilot about it so he didn’t have to bug me for the answer. Copilot confidently answered his question … and cited a presentation that I provided to my previous team as its primary reference! It wasn’t even a PowerPoint presentation – Copilot scanned the transcript of the meeting as a knowledge source, and it provided a link to the Teams video recording of the meeting (which was intended and treated as an informal knowledge share session). I might understand this if the question was about some kind of internal process specific to our organization, but it was about an internationally-recognized standard in our field. The answer to his question can be found on the internet.
q

In this case, the information that I provided in the presentation was accurate, but I am spiraling a bit wondering about the ways this could have gone awry! What if somebody else in a completely unrelated department searched for something related to my old job and somehow made a decision based on wrong or out-of-context information? What if they looked through the entire transcript and took offense to something we joked about during a meeting? Some of our internal stakeholders can be prickly, and we sometimes use meetings to blow off some steam in ways that might be offensive to the subjects of discussion. We’re not jerks about it – the discussion would be more like “yep, I’ve worked with Fergus too and know what he’s like! I hate getting his tickets during my on-call shift,” not “man, I hate Fergus.”
q

I am consistently praised on my professionalism but am not a perfect human. I’d hate for an executive or internal customer to somehow get a poor impression of me based on a Copilot response that is taken out of context. Am I overthinking this?
p

You’re overthinking the part about “what if someone made a decision based on wrong or out-of-context information?” That’s a risk of Copilot in general; it could just as easily get wrong or outdated information on the internet as it could from meeting transcripts.
p

But the rest, no — your team presumably wasn’t assuming those meeting transcripts would be available to other teams, let alone mined by AI. It’s worth suggesting excluding them from the resources that are available to be searched by Copilot.

3. Should you be able to get a cost-of-living raise if you recently got a merit raise?
q

I work for local government, and each year the employees usually get a standard cost-of-living increase across the board. However, when an employee has received a merit increase during the year, one of the personnel committee thinks that employee should not get a COL increase on top of that because they shouldn’t get two raises in one year.
q

I don’t think this is fair to punish someone for doing a good job but I don’t know whether this is normal. The cutoff seems to be about six months; that is, if the merit increase occurred more than six months ago, the committee member thinks the cost-of-living increase is okay, but if it is less than that, they shouldn’t get it. What do you think?
p

They’re in the wrong. Merit increases are an entirely separate thing from cost-of-living increases. Cost-of-living increases are intended to keep your salary the same in real dollars/earning power; they’re an adjustment because of inflation, not an increase to your actual buying power. Merit raises are intended to actually pay you more in real dollars. If you can’t get a cost-of-living raise after a merit raise, then your “merit raise” is actually much smaller than was intended because it’s not getting adjusted for inflation. That stance is unfair, bad for morale, and out of sync with what a merit raise is supposed to accomplish.
p
I wonder if your colleague understands that COL raises are solely about keeping pace with inflation.

4. Is it lying to not mention a promotion on my resume?
q

At my last job, I worked as a lab technician for just under a year before getting promoted to lab supervisor. I was in that job for a year and a half before getting laid off. The jobs were very similar, with the main difference being that I had two employee reports as a supervisor, I approved inventory orders, and I had to make sure we stayed in compliance with various regulations.
q

I’m worried that having two very short jobs listed on my resume, versus one longer job, looks worse and is hurting my job hunting prospects. Since I’m not interested in future supervisory positions anyway, would it be lying to ignore the supervisor promotion and list lab tech for the two-ish years?
p

It doesn’t look bad to have two shorter-term positions if they’re one after another at the same company; it’s clear that you were promoted from one role to the other. You’re thinking of job-hopping, where you move companies frequently. This is not that, and doesn’t reflect badly on you. If anything, it reflects well on you that your employers saw your work and decided to give you a higher level of responsibility. So if that’s the reason you’re considering leaving the supervisor title off, you shouldn’t.
p

On the other hand, if you wanted to leave that title off for a different reason — like that you actively don’t want to supervise anyone in the future and don’t want employers considering you for that — it would be fine to do. You can’t do it in other direction (claim you had a higher title for the whole period, when you only had it for part of that time) but you can just call yourself a lab tech for the whole period if you want to. If a reference checker verifies your title and hears “actually, she was promoted to lab supervisor in April,” it’s not going to look like you were trying to inflate anything. (Although you couldn’t do that if the actual work you were doing was wildly different — like if you moved from lab technician to bookkeeper.)
